Lesson 1 (08/09) explanatory notes
This first lesson (08/09, Verona & Mignini) opens Corporate Venturing and Innovation Strategy, a
course about technology strategy seen from inside the firm. The point of view is that of the leaders
who decide what a company does with technology: the R&D director, the head of corporate
development (make or buy) and the corporate venturing manager. Before talking about firms, the
session asks why everyone is so obsessed with innovation: industrialization changed the slope of
world growth, and the main growth theories (Schumpeter, Solow, Romer, the 2025 Nobel laureates
Mokyr, Aghion and Howitt) all put technological change at its core. Dosi then explains how the
direction of innovation is channelled, and the chain discoveries → inventions → innovations links
science to business. No recording exists for this date: the notes follow the slides and the core ideas of
the readings (Schumpeter's Theory of Economic Development, Dosi 1982). For the exam, focus on the
takeaway sentences of each slide and on applying the frameworks to AI and to incumbents.

The Course: Technology Strategy from Inside the Firm
The mission is to understand how firms use technology and innovation to position themselves
strategically, with particular attention to the AI transformation, treated as the latest instance of a long
history of technological revolutions. The content has two blocks: first, how technological change
affects firms and industries (industrial revolutions, dominant designs, demand dynamics,
organizational inertia); second, how firms organize and manage innovation (corporate R&D,
ambidexterity, corporate venturing, open innovation, make-or-buy). The required reading O'Reilly and
Tushman (2008) on ambidexterity belongs to the second block. Learning outcomes are phrased as
interpret, evaluate, recommend: exam questions rarely want a purely macroeconomic answer, and
even growth theory should end with what a manager learns from it.

Why Innovation: Growth Changed Slope
Using Maddison Project and Our World in Data reconstructions, the slides show average annual growth
of real world GDP by era: 0.17% in 1000–1700 (preindustrial), 0.52% in 1700–1820 (transition), 1.58% in
1820–1950 (industrial) and 3.70% in 1950–2022 (modern). This is a structural break: modern growth is
about 22 times the preindustrial rate. The First Industrial Revolution starts around 1760, but its global
effect compounds only after 1820. The takeaway on the slide: industrialization changed the slope,
from tenths of a percent to sustained multi-percent growth. Slope matters: at 0.17% output doubles in
about four centuries, at 3.7% in about 19 years. Each bar is a compound growth rate, not a GDP level.

Schumpeter: Innovation as the Engine
Joseph Schumpeter (1883–1950) put innovation at the core of the economy. In The Theory of
Economic Development (1911, English 1934) he starts from a static equilibrium, the circular flow, where
profits are competed away. Development is not gradual growth of population or savings but a
discontinuous change from within the system, whose source is innovation, defined as the carrying
out of new combinations: (1) a new good or quality, (2) a new method of production, (3) a new market,
(4) a new source of supply, (5) a new organization of an industry (creating or breaking a monopoly).
Innovation is therefore broader than new products.
The agent is the entrepreneur, distinct from the inventor (who produces ideas) and the capitalist (who
provides funds and bears financial risk): the entrepreneur actually introduces the new combination,
overcoming habit and social resistance, and is an entrepreneur only while doing so. Bank credit lets
him withdraw resources from existing uses. The reward is entrepreneurial profit, a temporary surplus
eroded by imitators. This is the seed of creative destruction (Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy,
1942): new combinations displace the old, creating winners and losers. For a manager, innovation is
the only durable source of above-normal profits, but those profits are temporary. Note the tension that
runs through the course: in the early Schumpeter the innovator is the new entrant, in the later
Schumpeter large firms with organized R&D.

Solow and Romer: Technology Outside and Inside the Model
Robert Solow (1957, Nobel 1987) built an exogenous growth model. With diminishing returns to
capital, accumulating machines cannot sustain per-capita growth forever: sustained growth requires gA
> 0, continuous technological progress. Measured as what remains after subtracting the contributions
of capital and labour, gA is the Solow residual (total factor productivity growth), which explains most of
the growth of output per worker; but its growth is assumed, not explained.

The 2025 Nobel: Useful Knowledge and Creative Destruction
The 2025 Nobel Prize was awarded for having explained innovation-driven economic growth: half to
Joel Mokyr, half jointly to Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt. Mokyr asks why progress became selfsustaining after the Industrial Revolution. Useful knowledge has two parts: prescriptive knowledge
(the how: recipes, designs, techniques) and propositional knowledge (the why: scientific
explanations). When they interact, techniques improve systematically rather than by trial and error; in
addition, society must be open to new ideas and tolerant of change, because innovation always
threatens someone.
Aghion and Howitt formalize growth through replacement, based on creative destruction. Firms
invest in R&D to climb a quality ladder, earn temporary monopoly profits with the better technology,
and are then displaced by a new entrant, which starts the next R&D race. Competition, entry and R&D
incentives determine the growth rate.

Dosi: Technological Paradigms and Trajectories
If markets and science both push innovation, what sets its direction? Giovanni Dosi (1982, Research
Policy) rejects both demand-pull (innovation follows market needs signalled by prices) and
technology-push (it follows autonomous science) as insufficient: direction emerges from selection,
learning and feedback. A technological paradigm is a shared model and pattern of solution of
selected technological problems, based on selected principles from natural science and selected
material technologies; it defines the relevant problems, knowledge, heuristics and dimensions of
progress. A technological trajectory is the pattern of normal, cumulative problem-solving within a
paradigm.

Figure 2 Dosi's framework: from an open opportunity space to a paradigm, a trajectory and market selection

The framework reads as a funnel: an opportunity space fed by science, the economy, institutions and
bottlenecks; focusing forces (feasibility, marketability, profitability, public priorities); the paradigm;
cumulative progress along the trajectory; and market selection, where winners accumulate knowledge
and scale and the industry moves to oligopolistic maturity. Two features matter for the course.
Learning is path-dependent: firms get good at improving along their trajectory, and switching can
mean starting again, which is why incumbents struggle when a paradigm changes. And a paradigm
shift is a discontinuity (Dosi borrows Kuhn's scientific revolutions) that resets the problem space;
within a paradigm, the paradigm acts as an exclusion device that makes engineers blind to
alternatives. Dosi's example: semiconductors, from vacuum tubes to transistors to integrated circuits.
Slide takeaway: markets influence innovation, but paradigms determine what engineers can see,
pursue and improve. Trap: Dosi is neither demand-pull nor technology-push.

Superinnovation: Three Forces Converging
The opening slide is a triangle with superinnovation at its centre and three vertices: (A) computing
power, (B) big and small data, (C) algorithms. Today's AI revolution is not a single breakthrough but
three streams of progress, each with a long history, that now reinforce one another: algorithms need
data to learn and computing power to be trained and run; data become valuable only when algorithms
extract patterns; computing is demanded because algorithms and data keep growing. In Lesson 1's
vocabulary, each vertex has its own trajectory, and their convergence opens a new paradigm.

Computing Power: From Transistors to GPUs and Beyond
The building blocks of the third industrial revolution are the transistor, the integrated circuit and the
microprocessor. The slides show two 1959 mainframes: Honeywell's first and the Elea 9003 built by
Olivetti in Pisa, the first mainframe with transistors, an Italian contribution Verona likes to stress.
Gordon Moore (co-founder of Fairchild in 1957 and Intel in 1968) gave his name to Moore's law:
transistors per chip double roughly every two years, so computing grows exponentially while its cost
falls. It is an empirical regularity, not a physical law, and a good example of a Dosi trajectory within
the semiconductor paradigm.
Today CPUs are complemented by GPUs. Nvidia's architectures (Hopper H100, Blackwell) power most
global AI infrastructure; systems like the Vera Rubin NVL72 cluster thousands of GPUs into a single
liquid-cooled machine, and Nvidia even targets satellites and orbital data centers. Nvidia's market value
overtook Apple and Microsoft in 2024 and reached $6.2 trillion in September 2026: the supplier of the
key input of the AI paradigm became the world's most valuable company. Computing also spreads to
the edge: the IoT sensor market grows from $10.9bn (2022) to $22.1bn (2027), and North American
wearables grow at a 12.9% CAGR (2025–2030); these devices both use computing and generate the
data of the second force. In the long run the slides look beyond silicon: quantum computing replaces
bits with qubits in superposition (measurement destroys it), and supercomputers already blend bits
and qubits (the ENI supercomputer in Pavia); organoid intelligence, biocomputing with brain-like
tissue, is a possible answer to the energy problem, since silicon computing approaches limits that
make its energy demand unsustainable.

Networks and Data: Information and Relations at the Fingertips
Machines become transformative when connected. On 29 October 1969 Leonard Kleinrock's group at
UCLA sent the first ARPANET message to the Stanford Research Institute; in 1991 Tim Berners-Lee
introduced HTTP, and in 1993 the Web became public as the World Wide Web. Bob Metcalfe cocreated Ethernet at Xerox in 1974; the timeline milestones (1993, 2005, 2007, 2010: public Web, social
platforms, smartphone, mobile apps and tablets) each multiplied the data generated by people and
devices.

Algorithms: From Predictive to Generative AI

brought information and relations; AI brings skills. Two dates: around 2015 predictive AI scales with
IoT data (forecasting demand, failures, risk); in 2022 generative AI reaches a mass audience with
ChatGPT, which had 800 million+ weekly users by December 2025.

Superinnovation at Work, Trust and Technological Anxiety
The applications reach sectors outside tech. Ant Group, 3-1-0: three minutes to apply for a loan, one
second to approve, zero humans involved; small businesses ignored by banks get credit decided by
algorithms on payment-platform data, scored by algorithms, run on cloud computing (all three forces).
Its motto: develop digital technology to serve the real economy. Waymo robotaxis in San Francisco

Digital twins, presented through David Teece (father of dynamic capabilities) at the SMS conference,

Lessons 1 and 2 left one question open: if innovation is the engine of growth, who produces it inside
the economy and how should an established company organise itself to keep producing it? This

The Productivity Crisis and the Shift of Paradigms
Exhibit 6: R&D spending by US pharma rose from about $3bn (1982) to about $40bn (2005), while new
chemical entities fell from close to 60 in the mid-1980s to about 20 a year in 2003–2005 (approximate
chart readings): more input, less output, the R&D productivity crisis. Its drivers: (1) easy targets were
taken, so trials were longer and larger; (2) imitation: science diffused quickly and rivals developed metoo drugs, so the median market exclusivity of a breakthrough fell from 10.2 years (1970s) to 1.2
years (late 1990s) (Inderal 10.7 years, Prozac 4.0, Celebrex 0.4 before Vioxx); (3) generics: nominal
patents of 17–20 years gave an effective life of 11–12 years, and after the Hatch-Waxman Act (1984)
sales collapsed within months of expiry; generics reached 56% of US volume but only 13% of value in
2005, and 19 blockbusters would go off patent by 2010; (4) the industry's focus on reformulations: only
about 14% of 1998–2002 FDA approvals were a significant improvement. Drug stocks fell 25% in five
years while biotech soared.

Radical Innovation and the Dominant Design
Product innovation is incremental (improving an existing product along known lines) or radical (a
product that did not exist and changes how a need is met, e.g. the first iPhone in 2007). The key claim:
radical product innovation favours the emergence of a dominant design, or product standard. A
dominant design is a product design adopted by the majority of producers, typically creating a stable
architecture on which the industry can focus its efforts (Shane 2009, on the slide); it presents
attributes liked by consumers and other stakeholders and is not necessarily the technically best
design. Classic standards: the VCR, the TV set, the Ford Model T, the QWERTY Underwood typewriter,
the PC, the iPod, the iPhone.
Radical innovations can fail. The Segway sold only 140,000 units at a launch price of $5,000, needed
a balancing learning curve that caused accidents, and lost the personal-mobility market to electric
scooters. LaserDisc (December 1978, two years after VHS, four before the CD) sold about 3.6 million
players before being discontinued in 2009. Successful ones: aspirin, the Web, X-ray imaging,
passenger aviation. Radical novelty is not enough if the product does not gather users, complements
and a mass-market price.

Dominant Designs Reshape Innovation: Abernathy and Utterback
The kind of innovation that matters changes over an industry's life, and the hinge is the dominant
design: first firms compete on what the product should be, then on how to make it cheaply and
reliably. In the fluid phase many firms experiment with different configurations, product innovation is
high, production uses general-purpose equipment, competition is on functional performance and entry
is easy. In the transitional phase a dominant design emerges, losing designs exit, the industry
consolidates and process innovation peaks. In the specific phase the product is standardised,
production capital-intensive and rigid, innovation incremental on cost and quality, and a few large firms
compete on price; this rigidity makes it vulnerable to a radical innovation that restarts the cycle.

From Atari's Boom to Nintendo's Dominant Design
The industry began in a textbook fluid phase: Magnavox Odyssey (1972, $100, about 100,000 units),
Atari's arcade and home Pong (Sears sold 150,000+ at $100 in 1975; about 75 Pong clones by 1977).
The decisive architectural step was separating console and software: Fairchild's Channel F (1976)
introduced interchangeable cartridges; Atari's VCS 2600 (1977) inverted the computer makers' model,
selling the console at $199, near cost, and cartridges costing under $10 at $30. Atari sold 15 million
VCS in 1979–1982 with an 80% share after the licensed hit Space Invaders.
The videogame bust of 1983
After the 1982 peak the industry lost 97% of annual sales volume in three years. Atari had not
locked out unauthorised developers: 100+ independents flooded the VCS with 1,000+ games of
variable quality, mostly paying no royalties. Only five or six of 130+ software firms survived; Atari
lost $539m, $40 games sold at $4, and six million unsold ET cartridges went to a landfill. The bust
was a failure of platform governance: too many low-quality complements destroyed the value of
the system.

Nintendo revived the industry with the Famicom (1983) and the NES (US 1985, $249, sold at an
operating loss) and Super Mario. It kept razor-and-blades but added control: an authentication chip in
every cartridge, royalties from third parties, the Seal of Quality, approval of every game and a cap of
five games per developer per year. By about 1990 the NES was in one in three US homes and
Nintendo held 90% of the market. This is the industry's dominant design: not a chip but an
architecture of product and business model (dedicated console on the TV, interchangeable games,

Supply Side: From Carriages to Cars
On 29 January 1886 Carl Benz applied for patent 37435 for a vehicle powered by a gas engine, the
birth certificate of the automobile. A patent does not settle the standard: three technologies competed,
steam, electric and endothermic (internal combustion), the fluid phase of Abernathy–Utterback. The
combustion engine won through production and selling choices: in 1909 Henry Ford decided to build
only the Model T, with one chassis (any colour so long as it is black), against his sales people's advice.
Standardisation lowered cost, lower cost expanded the market, and the market locked in the design.
Yet GM (founded 1908) took the lead by 1927 with Sloan's portfolio of brands, a car for every purse
and purpose: once the design is stable, competition moves to segmentation and variety around a
stable core, and the first mover is not guaranteed lasting leadership. Today cars are again in a fluid
phase (endothermic, hybrid, plug-in, electric, hydrogen): nobody can tell which will win, and the
outcome depends on aligning production, infrastructure and customers.

Successful Radical Innovations and Technology Trajectories
Kim Clark (1985): a radical innovation becomes a dominant design when three elements line up. Form
is the set of key product parameters; context is the socio-economic environment (above all customer
preferences) and the technological environment; fit is the ability to adapt the form to the context of
demand and supply under uncertainty and instability. Clark is the hinge of the session: a design wins
by fitting demand as well as supply.
Richard Foster's S-curve (McKinsey; evidence from chemical R&D) plots performance against
cumulative development effort (not time): slow improvement while basic knowledge is built, rapid
improvement once key problems are understood, then flattening near physical limits. The slope is the
return on extra R&D; an incumbent on the flat top gets diminishing returns, while an attacker on a new
S-curve can overtake it (Innovation: The Attacker's Advantage). Moore's law is the best-known
trajectory: processor performance grew about 25% a year until the mid-1980s, 52% in 1986–2002,
then about 20%: itself an S-curve on a log scale. Eli Lilly led insulin along one dimension, purity:
impurities fell from 50,000 ppm (1921) to 10,000 (1970) to 10 ppm (1980). Once a dominant design
exists, competition is continuous improvement along a trajectory, a supply-side story that does not
explain how customers take up the product.

Network Externalities: Metcalfe's Law and WhatsApp

Kodak's Success in Traditional Photography
George Eastman founded Kodak in Rochester in 1880, replaced glass plates with roll film (1884) and
launched the first Kodak camera (1888) with the slogan You press the button, we do the rest: the
customer takes pictures, Kodak sells everything afterwards. Its principles lasted a century: mass
production at low cost, international distribution, heavy advertising, customer focus, growth through
research. The core was a razor-blade model: cheap cameras build an installed base, profits come from
repeated sales of the consumable (film, chemicals, paper, processing). No matter what they said, they
were a film company. Equipment was ok as long as it drove consumables. Every new product was
judged by one question, does it drive consumables?, and digital would eliminate the consumable.
Barriers to entry were enormous: color film work since 1921, over $120 million spent by 1963, emulsion
chemistry and manufacturing know-how; Kodak's photo-finishing process became the industry
standard. Kodak controlled a system (film, chemistry, paper, retailers and photo-finishers) held
together by brand and marketing. Sales reached $1bn in 1962 and $10bn in 1981; by 1976 Kodak had
90% of US film and 85% of US camera sales. The organization mirrored success: power in Kodak
Park (the film plant), CEOs from manufacturing with identical training, avoidance of risk and
procedures and policies to maintain the status quo. Every ingredient is an asset in a stable regime and
a liability when it changes: silver-halide film was a mature dominant design in the specific phase.

Early Signals: Mavica, Fuji and the Photo CD
In August 1981 Sony announced the Mavica, the first commercial electronic still camera (analog, not
yet digital: 570×490 pixels, 50 frames on a diskette, viewed on TV). Kodak reacted with my goodness,
photography is dead: the threat was recognized immediately; the problem was never detection but
response. From 1983 to 1993 Kodak diversified away from photography into chemistry-like
businesses (Sterling Drug for $5.1bn, clinical diagnostics, copiers), defining itself by its chemistry.
Meanwhile Fuji attacked the core: 20% cheaper supplies, the first 400-speed color film (1976), the
1984 Olympics sponsorship Kodak refused (December 7th at Kodak), 21% of world film by 1993;
Kodak shelved its disposable camera because it clashed with the razor-blade model.
The paradox: Kodak was a digital pioneer. In 1986 it introduced the world's first electronic image
sensor (1.4 million pixels), launched 50+ electronic imaging products by 1989 and spent about $5bn

on digital research by 1993 (R&D 6.5–9% of sales); Apple's QuickTake used Kodak's sensor. But, in

Why Fisher's Transformation Failed
In late 1993 Kodak hired its first outsider CEO, George Fisher (ex-Motorola, Bell Labs), who said Kodak
was built on imaging, not film. His strategy: focus (divesting health, Sterling Drug, Eastman Chemical),
imaging, and China as a film market ($1.2bn of joint ventures in 1998; 63% of Chinese retail film and
7,000 Kodak Express stores by 2002). In 1994 he separated digital from silver-halide in a division led
by Carl Gustin (ex-DEC and Apple), launched re-engineering (cycle times ×10 in three years) and
wanted Kodak in all five links of the imaging chain.

very top but not the huge mass of middle managers, in a culture where everybody looked to the guy

The Rationale of Competence-Destroying Cycles

Figure 1 Tushman and Anderson's technology cycle applied to photography

In Tushman and Anderson (1986) a competence-enhancing discontinuity builds on existing knowhow and reinforces incumbents (black-and-white to color film); a competence-destroying one makes
it obsolete and favours entrants (silver-halide chemistry to digital electronics). The same technology
can be enhancing for one firm and destroying for another: digital built on Sony's electronics and
destroyed Kodak's chemistry. Slide examples: horses and carriages → cars; physical retail → ecommerce; physical music → digital files. The incumbent's curse slides show Porter's value chain next
to a tree whose deep roots are core competences, then two identical trees, one green (core
competences), one grey (core rigidities): rigidities are the same roots seen after the environment has
changed (Leonard-Barton). Two further sources of inertia: hierarchies (structural inertia: power,
careers, resource allocation built around the old core, e.g. CEOs from Kodak Park and resistant middle
managers) and cognition (managers read the new environment through the old mental model, money
comes from consumables; Tripsas and Gavetti found the same at Polaroid). Christensen's Innovator's
Dilemma explains why rational resource allocation to the best customers starves disruptive
businesses; O'Reilly and Tushman's ambidexterity is the remedy Kodak failed to sustain.

The Ukraine Shock and the Energy Trilemma
With the invasion of Ukraine, Europe realised that the king is naked: everything assumed gas would be
available, and no monetary or fiscal policy fixes a physical shortage. In 2021 83% of EU gas was
imported from outside the EU, about half from Russia; Italy's dependence on Russia was about 40%
(28bcm of about 65bcm consumed). New CEO Stefano Venier (April 2022) got the government call:
Houston, we have a problem. His diagnosis: the Green Deal had treated energy as abundant and
secure, so the only challenge seemed sustainability; the war showed that strategy must balance the
energy trilemma: security (diverse sources and routes), sustainability (decarbonisation) and
affordability (competitive prices). Beside Bill Gates's green premium there is a security premium.
Even at net zero about 50% of energy will still be molecules (Europe today is 75% molecules, 25%
electricity), and unlike past transitions, which added sources, this one tries to replace them; physics is
not digital. Management's stance: visionary pragmatism (decarbonisation as the goal, gradual and
country-specific paths) and technological agnosticism (no silver bullet, keep options open).

exploration simultaneously; in its structural form exploratory units have their own structures,
incentives and cultures but are integrated at the senior level to leverage the core's assets (brand,
customers, distribution); without that leverage a separate unit is just a weaker start-up. It is a dynamic
capability, not a structure, requiring a compelling strategic intent, a common vision and values, a
senior team with common-fate rewards, separate but aligned architectures with targeted integration,
and leaders able to manage contradictions.

From a Failed Taste Test to a Business
Dietrich Mateschitz, an Austrian sales and marketing manager, discovered in Asia that a local energy
drink, Krating Daeng (sugar, taurine, caffeine), wiped out his jet lag. In 1984 he acquired the rights
outside Asia with Chaleo Yoodvidhya, each partner investing about $500,000 for 49% of Red Bull
Trading; he renamed it, designed the two-bulls can and needed 18 months and about 50 proposals to
choose Red Bull Gives You Wings. The market research was a disaster: people did not believe the
taste, the logo or the name. He launched anyway, on 1 April 1987 in Austria, a small market ideal for
testing concepts. First-year revenues were about $1.1m against nearly $1.4m spent, mostly on

an investor, anyone would put money into that: it makes sense only as an entrepreneur's bet on
building a brand.
Why did a product that tested so badly work? Not vision or caffeine, but the most logical answer: a test
is valid only if it replicates the real situation of use. Red Bull was tasted alone, like a soft drink, but it
took off as a mixer in bars and clubs (a stimulant with a depressant: drunk without getting drowsy).

professor then asked, provocatively, why companies test so much, and told the class to be cynical:
much extreme testing protects managers in front of shareholders, yet about 98% of new consumergoods launches fail. Information is needed, but it does not replace judgment.

Takeaways and the Ju-Jitsu Strategy
1. Tactics are important, but in the long run you need a strong value proposition: Monster used the
same tactics differently; what lasts is the brand.
2. Operational efficiencies keep you in the game, but you need more currencies (distribution, trust,
perception) to build long-term value.
3. Imitation is always a dangerous threat to competitive advantage and market profitability (150+

4. Price wars are seldom effective in driving others out: lose-lose, the only winner is the consumer.
5. Ju-jitsu works both ways: adopting it does not prevent competitors from using it against you.

four principles: focus on unoccupied niches; turn competitor strengths into weaknesses and vice

advertising, range?). Red Bull's Austrian production and on-premise focus created the dilemma for
Coke; Monster's big can at the same price created it for Red Bull, which could not follow without
destroying its premium.

probable cost synergies (commercial functions), and top management committed to give Pixar the
right level of independence (structure, compensation, incentives). Pixar worked with Disney, not
inside it, and the model was repeated with Marvel (2009), Lucasfilm (2012), BAMTECH and 21st

people, not numbers: ego, overconfidence, falling in love with the deal, thinking the target is run by

food deal he worked on, ~$5bn of debt at 7% cost about $1m a day, so months without good local

The Good Old Times and Their Hidden Costs
LEGO (from Danish leg godt, "play well") was founded in 1916; the bricks arrived in 1949 and the LEGO
system in 1958, built on injection molding with tolerances of a few microns, so any brick fits any other.
By 1980 about 70% of Western European families with children under 14 owned LEGO. The professor
asked what the market looked like. On demand, many children with a lot of free time; on supply, low
competition and high prices. The real challenge was that LEGO could not meet demand, so it had to
manage demand: choose what to produce and, above all, which customers to serve, something that
almost never happens.
What happens to a company that makes a lot of profit without competition? Costs go up (one more
person, one more consultant), efficiency goes down (people become "fed and happy") and, the
biggest problem, innovation goes down, because people are not used to managing problems. High
margins also attract competitors, but the deeper damage is to culture, responsiveness and speed. His
comparison was Gillette, which was "printing money" and could not respond to cheaper substitutes:
like running a marathon without training.

The Market Changes: External Causes of Decline
From 1993 several forces converged. The target changed: fewer children, with less free time
(everything is scheduled) and shorter attention spans. Electronics (PlayStation, Xbox) were substitutes
taking play time, while low-cost Asian producers were direct competitors pushing prices down and
offering huge variety. Licensing turned toys into a fashion business.

Manage for cash is the emergency room: cash is the blood, so cut anything that absorbs cash and is

The Quartz Crisis
For two centuries Switzerland dominated mechanical watchmaking: by 1940 Swiss exports were 80%
of the value of the global industry. Ironically, a group of Swiss firms built the first quartz prototype. A
quartz crystal driven by a circuit was, from the start, about 20 times more accurate than a handwound mechanical watch. Most Swiss makers did not believe quartz would replace centuries of
tradition and chose to race: they invested in making the mechanical watch more accurate. Japanese
firms (Seiko, Casio), strong in electronics, took over quartz and cut its price by a factor of 100. By
1974 Swiss ads mentioned quartz more than mechanical, firms retooled for quartz, and experts
predicted the mechanical watch would vanish within a decade.
The damage: the Swiss share of world export value fell from over 50% to under 30% within a
decade; by 1983 more than half of the watchmakers were bankrupt and two thirds of jobs gone. In
1982 Swiss quartz sales overtook mechanical, and SMH launched the Swatch, an artistic quartz watch
(50 million sold in five years). Then the unexpected: from the late 1980s mechanical demand grew
again, mechanical exports overtook quartz in 2002, and by 2008 Switzerland held 55% of global
export value: CHF 15.8bn against 7.1bn for Hong Kong, 70% mechanical, 19 consecutive quarters of
growth and 40% more employees than in 1992. The Swiss lost the battle for units but won back the
battle for value.
Quartz was competence-destroying for the Swiss: better on the dimension customers had always
used to judge a watch (precision), far cheaper, and built on electronics, which they did not master at
scale. Standard theory predicts displacement; the interest lies in what happened after that prediction
failed. Exam trap: racing on precision failed because the Swiss competed on the one dimension where
the new technology was unbeatable; late efficiency gains on a legacy technology only delay its end.

Retire, Retreat or Redefine
Raffaelli starts from technology-cycle theory: a discontinuity opens an era of ferment, the field
selects a dominant design, and incremental change follows. The old technology reaches its limit and
fades (Tushman and Anderson: "the dying technology provides the compost" for the new one).
Incumbents often attempt a technological race, even borrowing from the new technology (carburettors
adopting elements of fuel injection, sailing ships learning from steam), but usually only delay the end.
The literature offered two trajectories; Raffaelli adds a third.

Technology reemergence is the resurgence of substantive and sustained demand for a legacy
technology after a new dominant design has been introduced: demand first retrenches into a niche,

goal of "survival and contraction". The Swiss did retrench in the 1980s, but then grew faster than
quartz: that is the anomaly the paper explains.

What reemergence is not
Not resource partitioning (craft beer filling segments big brewers leave empty): the Swiss

Not simple status recategorization (grappa climbing the spirits hierarchy): watches had been the

Lessons for Innovation Strategy
Cycles can include rebirth. After retire and retreat, redefine is a third branch; other cases are vinyl
(ten straight years of revenue growth by 2015), fountain pens ($48m in 1960 → $7m in 1975 → $17m
by 2007), streetcars (33 US cities) and recreational sailing, so it is not only luxury. Dominant design
vs dominant market category: the movement barely changed, but a new market category (art, status,
heritage), the shared schema used to group competing products, moved the competitive boundary
away from quartz; only then could firms experiment and reinvest. A product that loses on the
dominant design can win again on the category.
Cognition can enable adaptation, not only block it. Earlier in the course managerial cognition was a
cause of failure (anchoring on old meanings); here deliberate work on values, identity, history and
metaphors let incumbents adapt to a competence-destroying innovation. It cuts both ways: the 1970s
insistence on the old meaning likely deepened the decline, so preparing for cognitive barriers may
matter as much as for technical ones. A different ambidexterity: many firms explored quartz in the
1980s and returned to mechanical in the 1990s while still producing quartz, a strategy of vacillation
between new and legacy technology (the Swatch funded survival, the mechanical watch the future).
Note the response was reactive, not proactive.

Exam Angle
Conditions for reemergence: a latent value that can be reactivated and recombined; values touching
identity beyond use-value; the ability to attach new meanings gradually (bridging); a distinct market
category separating the legacy technology from the new one. Limits: a single qualitative study; open
causality between supply-side actions and demand (luxury fever, incomes); unclear whether
retrenchment must always come first. Be ready to explain why quartz was a discontinuity and why
racing failed, how reemergence differs from displacement and retrenchment, why meaning comes
before market and before R&D, why the competitive set narrows while the customer base widens, and
how the case revises dominant design, cognition and ambidexterity. Takeaway: a legacy technology
that loses on function can win again on meaning.

Geopolitics and Italy's Higher-for-Longer Prices
Geopolitical conflicts, trade wars and regulatory instability (populism, questioning of international law)
reach energy through supply chains and markets; the first symptom is price volatility. For an investor
in long-lived assets stability of the rules comes first: ENGIE is really defocusing from North America
after the Trump administration changed the rules, and fears a European drift (with elections in France,
Italy, Spain, Germany) toward treating energy as national sovereignty, from market to regulation,
which she considers a bad solution.
Italy is among the most exposed: after Ukraine it replaced Russian gas with Algerian and other less
stable suppliers and LNG; it has no nuclear, imports about 95% of its gas, and produces much of its
electricity with gas. Because the power price is set by the marginal (most expensive needed) plant,
usually gas-fired, even cheap renewable power is sold at a gas-driven price, and every gas shock
passes into the bill; more renewables push gas out of the margin more often. The 2026 slides list two
prolonged wars, pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, Brent above $100, TTF around €80/MWh, EU
storage at about 70% (lowest since 2009), and scarce capital while grid investment must grow 50% by
2030. In 2026 the Italian gas price rose from about €30 to about €80/MWh and baseload power from
€100–150 to over €200/MWh. Unlike 2022 (very high but short), prices are higher for longer: business
plans built on a return to normal no longer hold, and Italian industry loses competitiveness.

ENGIE's Strategy: Electrification, Flexibility and Grids
Three convictions for the next five years, held together by an alliance of electrons and molecules:
electrification is underway and molecules are here to stay; flexibility is essential for resilience;
power grid investment will expand steadily. Ambition: the best energy transition utility, through a
balanced portfolio; her advice was to choose activities and then be very bold. Electrification means
utility-scale renewables: less gas dependence lowers prices. Gas cannot be switched off overnight
(long construction and permitting times), so the molecule must be made green (biomethane).
Flexibility matches unpredictable wind and sun with demand: a BESS (battery energy storage system)
is the way to put in a box the electricity and use it when you need it; battery costs are falling fast and
3–5 MW systems can sit on a customer's site. Grids: renewables plus storage are useless without
transmission, hence the strategic shift from gas networks to power infrastructure.

PPAs: The Heineken Case and 24/7 Contracts
A PPA is a long-term contract, usually 10–15 years, in which a producer sells the electricity of a
specific (typically renewable) plant to a consumer at a fixed price. It gives the customer predictable
cost, lower exposure to volatility and measurable decarbonization; an on-site PPA feeds power from
a plant at the customer's premises, an off-site PPA delivers a remote plant's output through the grid.
The producer manages the gaps between production and demand through the market and storage, and
gains a long-term customer.
Case: Heineken Ichnusa brewery, Assemini (Sardinia)
ENGIE built an 8.5 MW ground-mounted PV plant (single-axis trackers, about 16,000 modules)
producing about 15.6 GWh a year and avoiding about 4,000 t of CO2 a year. Two contracts: an onsite PPA under which about 45% of output is self-consumed, covering 100% of the brewery's
needs when the plant produces, and an off-site PPA sending the other 55% to a Heineken plant in
northern Italy. Result: one site fully green, another half green, at a price flat for 10 years and below
today's market average: a win-win. Most PPAs are purely off-site (ENGIE plants in the south supply
Amazon logistics sites; one deal with Google).

The limit of a traditional PPA is the profile: solar peaks around 1 pm and falls in winter, so a PV-only
PPA matches Heineken's demand hour by hour only 40% of the time. The frontier is the hybrid 24/7
PPA combining solar, wind and storage so that production follows demand, raising the hourly match to
75%. In practice it is a virtual scheme: PPAs on PV and wind plants plus a tolling contract on a battery,
combined by ENGIE's energy-management platform. Barriers: technical complexity, economics,
regulation, network constraints; opportunities: distinctive positioning, asset optimisation, customer
